newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb leaders try to unite after NATO raid.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb leaders try to unite after NATO raid.

text.p: Bosnian Serb leaders said on Saturday they would try to resolve an internal power struggle aggravated by a NATO raid on suspected war criminals.

Feuding leaders appeared together in the northern town of Banja Luka at a religious celebration as they sought to present a united front two days after a NATO arrest operation against two Serb suspects indicted for war crimes.

The United States and other Western governments praised the swoop as a breakthrough for peacemaking efforts in Bosnia. But Serb media, under the control of the nationalist leadership, portrayed the action as an attack on the Serb nation.
The Serbian Orthodox church, which has close links to the ultra-nationalist leadership, issued an appeal for unity among Serb leaders at a time of crisis.

Patriarch Pavle, the highest church authority, travelled to Bosnia's autonomous Serb republic to help mediate the conflict between Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic and hardliners loyal to ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.

"The patriarch appealed to all of us to try to search for solutions and that there should be no winners. We will respect this advice," said Momcilo Krajisnik, a main ally of Karadzic and member of Bosnia's collective presidency.
Serb media, controlled by Karadzic loyalists, have accused Plavsic of provoking political turmoil which allowed NATO to strike at the war crimes suspects.
Krajisnik said it was time for a show of unity. "We have many enemies who want to destroy the Serb republic and we have to be aware of it," he told official television.
Plavsic, who has slammed Krajisnik and Karadzic over alleged large-scale corruption, has condemned the NATO operation but her opponents were painting her as a pawn of Western powers.
Acting on orders from NATO commanders, British special forces arrested one suspect and shot dead another in a gun battle near the northwestern town of Prijedor on Thursday.
Both suspects were charged by the U.N. war crimes tribunal under sealed indictments in connection with a brutal campaign to purge Moslems and Croats from the Prijedor region early in the 1992-95 war.
"Operation Tango" broke new ground for the NATO-led peacekeeping mission which had previously ruled out going after suspects unless troops happened to stumble upon them.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said the raid was ordered to shore up the fragile peace agreed in Dayton, Ohio in 1995.
"We basically believe that we have to make an effort to save the Dayton process," Clinton told reporters on Friday.

U.S. and Western diplomats say prosecuting war crimes suspects is a crucial step in building post-war reconciliation and clearing the way for the scheduled withdrawal of peacekeeping troops within a year.

NATO declined to discuss whether there would be more arrests but the raid in Prijedor and the use of sealed indictments raised expectations that more suspects would be nabbed in Bosnia's Serb or Moslem-Croat entities.
The shift in tactics also fed speculation that the two most prominent suspects on the published list of indictments -- Karadzic and his former army commander General Ratko Mladic -- might be next.
